sentences.text: Bravoceratops was a large chasmosaurine ceratopsid with a distinctive narrow snout, a large frill formed by the squamosal and parietal bones with large elongated openings, large robust epijugal horns, and long horns over the brow.

The skull fossil includes fragments of the braincase, brow horns, postorbital, nasal area, jugals, quadrates, parietal, epiparietals, dentary, and squamosal, featuring a large flange in front of the quadrate near the jugal bones and compressed brow horns that are taller than wide.
This dinosaur displays a distinctive combination of traits not seen in any previously described chasmosaurine.
The specific name references a hollow in the parietal bar shaped like an inverted tear, resembling the single eye of the cyclops Polyphemus.
The discovery is significant because ceratopsian fossils are found only rarely in the Javelina Formation.
The only known specimen is the holotype TMM 46015-1, which consists of a fragmentary skull in good preservation and is housed in the collection of the Texas Memorial Museum in Austin, Texas.
The genus was named and described by Steven L. Wick and Thomas M. Lehman in 2013, with the name meaning horned face of the Rio Bravo, derived from the Rio Grande and Greek words for horn and face.

It was found in the strata of the Javelina Formation in Big Bend National Park in Texas, USA, within a conglomerate of sandstone sediments deposited at the beginning of the Maastrichtian stage, approximately 70 million years ago.
The various parts of the holotype skull were completely disarticulated and scattered over an area of approximately ten square meters before fossilization.
Many of the more robust remains, such as the horns, exhibit erosion and wear, suggesting the skull remained exposed for a time before being buried.
Bravoceratops was assigned to the subfamily Chasmosaurinae in 2013, belongs to the family Ceratopsidae, and is part of the class Ornithischia.

It is an intermediate chasmosaurine, more advanced than Chasmosaurus but less so than Triceratops, considered the sister taxon of Coahuilaceratops, and part of a clade endemic to the Southwestern United States, though its fragmentary nature often excludes it from phylogenetic analyses as an unstable wildcard taxon.
The presence of a midline epiparietal on the distal margin of the frill and the bifurcated squatoyugal–squamosal articulation in the skull are considered derived traits.

Bravoceratops lived about 70 million years ago in the Late Cretaceous Javelina Formation, during the Maastrichtian, from 72.2 to 66 million years ago, in a paleoenvironment of a river plain located several hundred kilometers inland, far from the nearest coastline.
In 2020, Fowler and Freedman Fowler suggested the genus was invalid because the parietal bar was likely reconstructed upside down, removing its distinguishing features.
